> **Re:** Audit Preliminary Findings --- Comprehensive Tax Audit
>
> **Case No.:** ODT-AUD-2023-07814 **Federal EIN:** 34-1987652 **Ohio Tax ID:** 00-874231 **Tax Types:** Commercial Activity Tax; Sales and Use Tax; Income Tax Withholding **Audit Period:** Tax Years Ending December 31, 2020, December 31, 2021, and December 31, 2022

Dear Ms. Chen:

**[I. Introduction and Audit Summary]{.underline}**

The Ohio Department of Taxation (\"Department\") has completed its field examination of the books, records, and tax returns of Greystone Industrial Holdings, Inc. (\"Taxpayer\") for the above-referenced audit period. This letter sets forth the Department\'s preliminary findings and proposed adjustments resulting from that examination. These findings are preliminary in nature and do not constitute a final determination of tax liability.

The audit was initiated on March 15, 2023, pursuant to the Department\'s examination authority under Ohio Revised Code (\"O.R.C.\") § 5703.19 and O.R.C. § 5747.13. The field audit was conducted at Taxpayer\'s corporate headquarters located at 4510 Brecksville Road, Suite 300, Richfield, Ohio 44286, during the period from April 2023 through January 2024. The examination was performed by Senior Tax Examiner Harold R. Pfeiffer, Badge No. 4417, under the supervision of Supervising Auditor Marjorie Kwan, Badge No. 3892, both of the Department\'s Audit Division.

The audit covered the following three Ohio tax types: (1) Ohio Commercial Activity Tax (\"CAT\"); (2) Ohio Sales and Use Tax; and (3) Ohio Income Tax Withholding. The examination encompassed the tax years ending December 31, 2020, December 31, 2021, and December 31, 2022.

During the course of the examination, the Department issued three Information Document Requests (\"IDRs\") to the Taxpayer: IDR No. 1 (issued May 3, 2023), IDR No. 2 (issued July 19, 2023), and IDR No. 3 (issued October 11, 2023). The Taxpayer provided responses to these IDRs on the following dates, respectively: May 31, 2023, August 14, 2023, and November 8, 2023. The Department acknowledges the Taxpayer\'s cooperation during the examination process and the timely submission of all requested documentation.

These preliminary findings set forth the Department\'s proposed adjustments to the Taxpayer\'s reported tax liabilities for the audit period. Pursuant to the Department\'s administrative procedures, the Taxpayer has sixty (60) days from the date of this letter --- that is, until **April 12, 2024** --- to submit a written protest before a Final Assessment Notice is issued. The procedures for submitting a written protest are described in Section VI of this letter.

As background, Greystone Industrial Holdings, Inc. is an Ohio corporation formed in 2004. The Taxpayer is a mid-market manufacturer of specialty coatings and adhesives with annual consolidated revenue of approximately \$187 million. The Taxpayer operates three manufacturing plants in the State of Ohio and sells its products to customers located in thirty-eight (38) states. The Taxpayer has two wholly owned subsidiaries: Greystone Coatings Southeast LLC, organized under the laws of the State of Georgia, and Greystone Adhesives West LLC, organized under the laws of the State of Nevada. Both subsidiaries were included within the scope of the Department\'s examination to the extent relevant to the Taxpayer\'s Ohio tax obligations.

**[II. Commercial Activity Tax (CAT) --- Proposed Adjustments]{.underline}**

The Department\'s examination of the Taxpayer\'s Ohio Commercial Activity Tax returns for tax years 2020, 2021, and 2022 identified underreported taxable gross receipts in each of the three tax years under examination. The proposed adjustments are set forth below.

**A. Tax Year 2020 --- CAT Adjustment**

The Department determined that the Taxpayer underreported taxable gross receipts by **\$4,215,000** for the tax year ending December 31, 2020. The underreported amount consists of intercompany management fees received by the Taxpayer from its two wholly owned subsidiaries: Greystone Coatings Southeast LLC (Georgia) and Greystone Adhesives West LLC (Nevada). These management fees were paid to the Taxpayer in consideration for centralized management, administrative, and operational support services provided from the Taxpayer\'s Ohio headquarters.

The Taxpayer excluded these intercompany management fees from its reported CAT taxable gross receipts, asserting that the fees were excludable under the related-member provisions of the CAT statute. The Department\'s position is that these fees constitute taxable gross receipts that are not excludable under the related-member exemption set forth in O.R.C. § 5751.01(F)(2). The Department interprets the exemption as inapplicable to management fees received from out-of-state affiliated entities under the facts and circumstances presented in this case, where the subsidiaries are organized and operating outside Ohio and the fees represent compensation for services performed in Ohio.

Proposed additional CAT for 2020: \$4,215,000 × 0.26% = **\$10,959.00**.

**B. Tax Year 2021 --- CAT Adjustment**

The Department determined that the Taxpayer underreported taxable gross receipts by **\$5,830,000** for the tax year ending December 31, 2021. This underreported amount consists of two components:

> \(a\) **Intercompany management fees of \$3,740,000** received from Greystone Coatings Southeast LLC and Greystone Adhesives West LLC, on the same basis as described in Section II.A above; and
>
> \(b\) **Licensing receipts of \$2,090,000** received from a Canadian distributor for the licensing of the Taxpayer\'s proprietary coating formulas. The Department determined that these licensing receipts constitute Ohio-sourced gross receipts under the CAT situsing rules set forth in O.R.C. § 5751.033, based on the Department\'s determination that the benefit of the licensed intangible property was received at the Taxpayer\'s Ohio location where the intellectual property was developed and managed.

Proposed additional CAT for 2021: \$5,830,000 × 0.26% = **\$15,158.00**.

**C. Tax Year 2022 --- CAT Adjustment**

The Department determined that the Taxpayer underreported taxable gross receipts by **\$6,410,000** for the tax year ending December 31, 2022. This underreported amount consists of two components:

> \(a\) **Intercompany management fees of \$4,120,000** received from Greystone Coatings Southeast LLC and Greystone Adhesives West LLC, on the same basis as described in Section II.A above; and
>
> \(b\) **Canadian licensing receipts of \$2,290,000**, on the same basis as described in Section II.B above.

Proposed additional CAT for 2022: \$6,410,000 × 0.26% = **\$16,666.00**.

**D. Total Proposed CAT Deficiency**

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Tax Year**            **Underreported Gross Receipts**   **Proposed Additional CAT**
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------- -----------------------------
  2020                    \$4,215,000                        \$10,959.00

  2021                    \$5,830,000                        \$15,158.00

  2022                    \$6,410,000                        \$16,666.00

  **Total**               **\$16,455,000**                   **\$42,783.00**
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

These preliminary findings do not compute penalties or interest with respect to the proposed CAT adjustments. Penalties and interest, if applicable, will be calculated and included in the Final Assessment Notice if the proposed adjustments are sustained.

The Department\'s legal basis for the foregoing adjustments rests upon O.R.C. § 5751.01(F)(2) regarding the definition of \"gross receipts\" and the scope of the related-member exclusion, and O.R.C. § 5751.033 regarding the situsing of gross receipts from licensing transactions with the Canadian distributor.

**[III. Sales and Use Tax --- Proposed Adjustments]{.underline}**

The Department\'s Sales and Use Tax Division identified four categories of proposed adjustments arising from its examination of the Taxpayer\'s Ohio sales and use tax returns and supporting documentation for the period January 2020 through December 2022. Each proposed adjustment is described below.

**A. Proposed Adjustment SUT-1: Failure to Collect Sales Tax on Shield Pro Coating Sales**

The Department\'s examination determined that the Taxpayer failed to collect Ohio sales tax on sales of its \"Greystone Shield Pro\" coating product to four Ohio-based customers during the period January 2021 through December 2022. The Taxpayer classified these four customers as \"industrial users\" entitled to claim exemption from Ohio sales tax and accepted blanket exemption certificates from each customer. However, the Department\'s review of the business activities of these four customers --- including examination of their Ohio commercial activity tax filings, publicly available business descriptions, and information obtained through third-party verification --- determined that these customers are retail resellers of the Shield Pro product, not end-use industrial consumers. Accordingly, the exemption certificates accepted by the Taxpayer were not valid for these transactions, and the Taxpayer was required to collect and remit Ohio sales tax on the subject sales.

The total taxable sales to these four customers during the period January 2021 through December 2022 were **\$1,847,500**. The proposed state sales tax on these sales is calculated as follows:

> State sales tax: \$1,847,500 × 5.75% = **\$106,231.25**

Additionally, the Department\'s records indicate that **\$623,000** of these sales were sourced to customer locations within Cuyahoga County, Ohio. The applicable Cuyahoga County transit authority surtax rate for the periods in question was 2.25%. The proposed county surtax is calculated as follows:

> Cuyahoga County surtax: \$623,000 × 2.25% = **\$14,017.50**

**Total Proposed SUT-1 Deficiency: \$106,231.25 + \$14,017.50 = \$120,248.75**

The \$623,000 figure representing sales sourced to Cuyahoga County locations was derived from the Department\'s analysis of the Taxpayer\'s sales invoices, shipping records, and delivery confirmations reviewed during the field examination.

**B. Proposed Adjustment SUT-2: Failure to Self-Assess Use Tax on Manufacturing Equipment**

The Department\'s examination determined that the Taxpayer purchased a specialty mixing and blending machine from Hartmann Maschinenbau GmbH, a German manufacturer, for a total acquisition cost of **\$2,340,000**. The machine was imported into the United States and installed at the Taxpayer\'s Richfield manufacturing plant in November 2021. No Ohio sales tax was collected at the time of purchase, and the Taxpayer did not self-assess Ohio use tax on the acquisition. The Taxpayer claimed a full manufacturing machinery and equipment exemption under O.R.C. § 5739.011.

The Department\'s position is that the mixing and blending machine is used approximately fifty percent (50%) for direct manufacturing production activities and approximately fifty percent (50%) for research and development activities. The Department contends that this dual-use nature disqualifies the machine from the full manufacturing exemption under O.R.C. § 5739.011, which requires that qualifying equipment be \"primarily used\" in the manufacturing operation. Because the machine does not meet the \"primarily used\" standard, the Department proposes to assess use tax on fifty percent (50%) of the purchase price --- the portion attributable to non-qualifying research and development use.

Proposed use tax assessment:

> Taxable portion: \$2,340,000 × 50% = \$1,170,000
>
> State use tax rate: 5.75% Summit County use tax rate: 1.00% Combined rate: 6.75%
>
> Proposed use tax: \$1,170,000 × 6.75% = **\$78,975.00**

**C. Proposed Adjustment SUT-3: Taxable Installation and Repair Services**

The Department\'s examination determined that the Taxpayer\'s field service technicians provided installation and repair services to Ohio-based customers during the audit period of January 1, 2020 through December 31, 2022. The Taxpayer treated the revenue from these services as non-taxable. The Department reclassified these services as taxable \"repair and installation\" services under O.R.C. § 5739.01(B)(3), which includes within the definition of taxable sales the provision of repair, installation, and maintenance services performed on tangible personal property belonging to others.

The Department examined the Taxpayer\'s service invoicing records for the period January 1, 2020 through December 31, 2022, including quarterly service revenue summaries. The following service revenue figures were identified:

> **Tax Year 2020: \$132,100**
>
> The 2020 figure of \$132,100 includes service revenue from all four quarters of the calendar year, as follows:
>
> • Q1 2020 (January--March): \$31,400
>
> • Q2 2020 (April--June): \$29,700
>
> • Q3 2020 (July--September): \$34,200
>
> • Q4 2020 (October--December): \$36,800
>
> **Tax Year 2021: \$138,200**
>
> **Tax Year 2022: \$147,300**
>
> **Total Service Revenue (Preliminary): \$132,100 + \$138,200 + \$147,300 = \$417,600**

The quarterly breakdown of the 2020 service revenue is noted here because the sales tax return filing due dates for each quarterly period determine the applicable assessment periods. Specifically, the Q1 2020 service revenue of \$31,400 corresponded to a sales tax return due date of April 23, 2020, and the Q2 2020 service revenue of \$29,700 corresponded to a sales tax return due date of July 23, 2020. The Q3 2020 and Q4 2020 returns were due on October 23, 2020 and January 23, 2021, respectively.

Proposed state sales tax on installation and repair services:

> \$417,600 × 5.75% = **\$24,012.00**

**D. Proposed Adjustment SUT-4: Failure to Remit Collected Sales Tax (Q3 2022)**

The Department\'s records indicate that the Taxpayer collected **\$83,412.00** in Ohio sales tax from its customers during the third quarter of 2022 (July through September 2022). However, the Taxpayer remitted only **\$61,917.00** for that reporting period. The resulting discrepancy between the amount of sales tax collected and the amount remitted is **\$21,495.00**.

The Department notes this discrepancy and states that the matter will be subject to further review regarding the appropriate penalty classification. The proposed deficiency for SUT-4 is the under-remittance amount of **\$21,495.00**. The characterization and application of any penalty with respect to this under-remittance will be determined in the Final Assessment Notice, if issued.

**E. Total Proposed Sales and Use Tax Adjustments --- Summary**

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Adjustment**          **Description**                                              **Proposed Deficiency**
  ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ -------------------------
  SUT-1                   Failure to Collect Sales Tax --- Shield Pro Sales            \$120,248.75

  SUT-2                   Failure to Self-Assess Use Tax --- Manufacturing Equipment   \$78,975.00

  SUT-3                   Taxable Installation and Repair Services                     \$24,012.00

  SUT-4                   Failure to Remit Collected Sales Tax (Q3 2022)               \$21,495.00

  **Total**                                                                            **\$244,730.75**
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**[IV. Income Tax Withholding --- Proposed Adjustments]{.underline}**

**Proposed Adjustment WHT-1: Failure to Withhold Municipal and School District Income Tax for Columbus Project Employees**

The Department\'s examination of the Taxpayer\'s payroll records and employee work assignment schedules determined that the Taxpayer assigned fourteen (14) employees from its Richfield manufacturing plant to a sixteen-month construction and installation project at AllBright Manufacturing, located at 1900 Scioto Trail, Columbus, Ohio 43215. The assignment spanned the period from March 2021 through June 2022. During this assignment, these employees performed their duties exclusively at the Columbus work site.

The Department determined that the Taxpayer did not withhold Columbus municipal income tax or Ohio School District income tax (Columbus City School District) for these fourteen employees during their assignment to the Columbus location. Instead, the Taxpayer continued to withhold only at the rates applicable to the Richfield work location (Village of Richfield and Revere Local School District) without adjusting for the Columbus work location withholding obligations.

Under O.R.C. § 5747.06 and applicable municipal tax provisions, employers are required to withhold income tax at the rate applicable to the jurisdiction in which the employee performs services. Because these fourteen employees performed their services at the Columbus, Ohio work site for the duration of the assignment, the Taxpayer was required to withhold Columbus municipal income tax and Columbus City School District income tax on the wages paid to these employees for services performed in Columbus.

The total wages paid to the fourteen assigned employees for services performed at the Columbus work site were as follows:

> 2021 (March through December): \$762,400 2022 (January through June): \$485,200 **Total wages subject to withholding: \$1,247,600**

The proposed withholding deficiencies are calculated as follows:

> Columbus municipal income tax: \$1,247,600 × 2.50% = **\$31,190.00** Columbus City School District income tax: \$1,247,600 × 0.50% = **\$6,238.00** **Total WHT-1 proposed deficiency: \$31,190.00 + \$6,238.00 = \$37,428.00**

The fourteen employees assigned to the Columbus project are identified by the following employee badge numbers as reflected in the Taxpayer\'s payroll records: Badge Nos. 2104, 2217, 2389, 2456, 2501, 2678, 2793, 2845, 2912, 3055, 3189, 3294, 3387, and 3401. The Department\'s proposed adjustment encompasses all wages paid to each of these fourteen employees for services performed at the Columbus work site during the assignment period.

**[V. Summary of All Proposed Adjustments]{.underline}**

The following table summarizes all proposed tax deficiencies identified in the Department\'s preliminary findings. These figures represent tax only and do not include penalties or interest, which will be computed and included in the Final Assessment Notice if the proposed adjustments are sustained.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Tax Type**                           **Proposed Deficiency**
  -------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Commercial Activity Tax (Section II)   \$42,783.00

  Sales and Use Tax (Section III)        \$244,730.75

  Income Tax Withholding (Section IV)    \$37,428.00

  **Total Proposed Deficiency**          **\$324,941.75**
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------

Penalties and interest applicable to the foregoing proposed adjustments will be calculated and assessed in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Ohio Revised Code and the Ohio Administrative Code. Estimated penalties and interest are not provided at this preliminary stage. However, the Department advises the Taxpayer that the combined grand total of tax, penalties, and interest is expected to exceed \$400,000 if all proposed adjustments are sustained and applicable statutory penalties and interest are applied.

**[VI. Taxpayer\'s Rights and Protest Procedures]{.underline}**

The Taxpayer has the right to submit a written protest to these preliminary findings. Any written protest must be received by the Department within sixty (60) days of the date of this letter --- that is, no later than **April 12, 2024**.

The written protest should be addressed to:

> Harold R. Pfeiffer Senior Tax Examiner, Badge No. 4417 Audit Division --- Commercial Activity Tax & Income Tax Section Ohio Department of Taxation 4485 Northland Ridge Boulevard Columbus, Ohio 43229

The written protest should specifically identify each proposed adjustment being contested, set forth the factual and legal basis for the Taxpayer\'s disagreement, and include all supporting documentation and legal authority upon which the Taxpayer relies. The Taxpayer is encouraged to provide as complete a response as possible to facilitate the Department\'s review.

If no written protest is received within the sixty-day period, or if the Department does not accept the arguments set forth in the Taxpayer\'s protest, a Final Assessment Notice will be issued. Upon issuance of a Final Assessment Notice, the Taxpayer will have sixty (60) days from the date of the Final Assessment Notice to file a Petition for Reassessment with the Ohio Tax Commissioner under O.R.C. § 5717.02. The Taxpayer is advised that the filing of a Petition for Reassessment is a prerequisite to further administrative or judicial review.

The Taxpayer has the right to be represented by legal counsel or an authorized agent at any stage of the audit, protest, and assessment process. The Department is also available for an informal conference to discuss these preliminary findings and the underlying factual and legal issues prior to the protest deadline. To schedule an informal conference, the Taxpayer or its representative should contact Senior Tax Examiner Harold R. Pfeiffer at the telephone number provided below.

**[VII. Information Reviewed During the Audit]{.underline}**

The following is a summary of the principal documents and records reviewed by the Department during the field examination:

> 1\. Greystone Industrial Holdings, Inc. --- Ohio Commercial Activity Tax returns for tax years 2020, 2021, and 2022, including all schedules and supporting workpapers.
>
> 2\. Greystone Industrial Holdings, Inc. --- Ohio Sales and Use Tax returns for the reporting periods January 2020 through December 2022, including monthly and quarterly filings.
>
> 3\. Greystone Industrial Holdings, Inc. --- Ohio employer income tax withholding returns for tax years 2021 and 2022, including IT-501 quarterly returns and IT-941 annual reconciliation returns.
>
> 4\. General ledger extracts and trial balances for all three tax years under examination.
>
> 5\. Intercompany management fee agreements between the Taxpayer and Greystone Coatings Southeast LLC and between the Taxpayer and Greystone Adhesives West LLC, including amendments and fee schedules.
>
> 6\. Licensing agreement between the Taxpayer and a Canadian distributor for the licensing of proprietary coating formulas, including royalty schedules and payment records.
>
> 7\. Blanket exemption certificates on file for Ohio customers, including the four customers identified in Proposed Adjustment SUT-1.
>
> 8\. Purchase documentation for the Hartmann Maschinenbau GmbH specialty mixing and blending machine, including purchase order, invoice, customs documentation, freight and insurance records, and installation records.
>
> 9\. Payroll records, employee work assignment schedules, and W-2 forms for the fourteen employees assigned to the AllBright Manufacturing construction project in Columbus, Ohio.
>
> 10\. All materials provided by the Taxpayer in response to Information Document Requests Nos. 1, 2, and 3.

This letter constitutes the Department\'s preliminary findings only and is not a final determination of tax liability. The proposed adjustments set forth herein are subject to modification based upon information provided by the Taxpayer during the protest period or as a result of further review by the Department. Please direct any questions or correspondence regarding these findings to the undersigned.

Respectfully,

Harold R. Pfeiffer Senior Tax Examiner, Badge No. 4417 Audit Division --- Commercial Activity Tax & Income Tax Section Ohio Department of Taxation 4485 Northland Ridge Boulevard Columbus, Ohio 43229 Telephone: (614) 555-0147

Email: h.pfeiffer@tax.ohio.gov

Reviewed and Approved by:

Marjorie Kwan Supervising Auditor, Badge No. 3892 Audit Division Ohio Department of Taxation

**Enclosures:** None

At no point during the Audit Period did Greystone alter its reporting position with respect to these fees, and at no point prior to the issuance of the Preliminary Findings did ODT communicate any concern regarding this treatment.
50	
51	If ODT\'s position were sustained, the resulting additional CAT liability would be as follows:

53	> • Tax Year 2020: \$10,959.00
54	>

56	>

64	>

66	
67	Greystone respectfully requests that ODT withdraw the CAT intercompany management fee adjustments in their entirety for all three tax years under audit. ODT\'s interpretation of O.R.C. § 5751.01(F)(2)(ll) as requiring Ohio domicile of the related member is without statutory basis, is inconsistent with the plain text of the statute, and would, if applied broadly, undermine the purpose of the related-member exclusion for any multi-state group with out-of-state subsidiaries.
68	
69	**[III. Protest Point Two: Hartmann Mixing Machine Qualifies for Full Manufacturing Exemption Under O.R.C. § 5739.011]{.underline}**
70	
71	The Preliminary Findings at item SUT-2 assess Ohio use tax on 50% of the purchase price of a specialty mixing and blending machine purchased by Greystone from Hartmann Maschinenbau GmbH, a German manufacturer of industrial processing equipment. The machine was installed at Greystone\'s Richfield manufacturing plant in November 2021. The total purchase price of the machine was \$2,340,000. ODT assessed use tax on \$1,170,000 (50% of the purchase price) at the combined state and county rate of 6.75% (state rate of 5.75% plus Summit County rate of 1.00%), resulting in a use tax deficiency of \$78,975.00.
72	
73	ODT\'s rationale for the partial assessment is that the machine has a \"dual use\" --- approximately 50% production and 50% research and development --- and that this dual use disqualifies the machine from the full manufacturing machinery and equipment exemption. ODT applied a pro-rata approach, granting a 50% exemption and assessing tax on the remaining 50%.
74	
75	Greystone contends that the Hartmann mixing machine qualifies for the full manufacturing exemption under O.R.C. § 5739.011, which provides an exemption for machinery and equipment used \"primarily\" in a manufacturing operation. The Hartmann machine is used in the manufacture and development of specialty industrial coatings, which is Greystone\'s core business. The R&D activities performed on the machine are integral to and inseparable from the manufacturing process itself. New formulations tested and developed on the machine are developed for the sole purpose of commercial production. These R&D activities are not academic or theoretical in nature; they are part of Greystone\'s continuous process of developing, testing, and refining commercial products for sale to customers.
76	
77	Ohio Administrative Code § 5703-9-21 interprets the manufacturing exemption broadly to encompass equipment used in activities that are part of the continuous manufacturing process, including equipment used in quality control, testing, and product development activities that are directly related to and supportive of manufacturing operations. The Hartmann machine falls squarely within this interpretation.
78	
79	Furthermore, ODT\'s pro-rata approach to the exemption --- granting a 50% exemption and taxing the remaining 50% --- has no explicit statutory basis. O.R.C. § 5739.011 applies an all-or-nothing \"primarily used\" test: if the equipment is used primarily in manufacturing, the full exemption applies. The statute does not authorize proportional allocation. If the machine is used 50% in direct production and 50% in R&D activities that are themselves part of the manufacturing function, then the machine is used 100% in manufacturing-related activities and qualifies for the full exemption.
80	
81	Greystone respectfully requests that ODT withdraw the SUT-2 assessment in its entirety, totaling \$78,975.00 in use tax deficiency, plus all allocable penalties and interest.

85	The Preliminary Findings at item SUT-3 reclassify installation and repair services allegedly provided by Greystone\'s field service technicians to Ohio customers as taxable \"repair and installation\" services under O.R.C. § 5739.01(B)(3). ODT assessed Ohio sales tax on the following service revenue for the Audit Period:

97	Greystone protests this assessment on the ground that the services provided by its field technicians are not taxable \"repair and installation\" services within the meaning of the statute. The activities performed by Greystone\'s field service technicians are properly characterized as application engineering and technical consulting services provided incidental to the sale of Greystone\'s coating products. These technicians provide guidance to customers on surface preparation, application parameters, curing protocols, and quality assurance procedures. Their function is to ensure that customers successfully apply Greystone\'s specialty coating products, not to install or repair tangible personal property.
98	
99	The revenue recorded by Greystone for these activities represents charges for technician time and travel expenses, not charges for the \"installation\" or \"repair\" of tangible personal property in the statutory sense. Greystone\'s technicians do not install or repair equipment; they supervise and assist customers in the application of coating products that the customers have purchased from Greystone. These are pre-sale and post-sale technical support services that are commonly understood to be non-taxable professional or consulting services. The services are more properly characterized as consulting or professional services, which are not enumerated as taxable services under O.R.C. § 5739.01(B). Ohio\'s sales tax applies only to specifically enumerated services, and the activities at issue do not fall within any enumerated category.
100	
101	Greystone respectfully requests that ODT withdraw the SUT-3 assessment in its entirety, totaling \$23,736.00 in sales tax deficiency, plus all allocable penalties and interest.

119	Greystone contests the Columbus municipal income tax component of this assessment on jurisdictional grounds. Under O.R.C. Chapter 718, municipal income tax in Ohio is administered by the individual municipality or by a regional collection agency such as the Regional Income Tax Agency (RITA) or the Central Collection Agency (CCA) for participating municipalities. The City of Columbus administers its own municipal income tax through the Columbus Division of Income Tax. ODT does not have statutory authority to assess Columbus municipal income tax. ODT\'s jurisdiction extends to state income tax withholding and school district income tax withholding, but the Columbus municipal income tax component of \$31,190.00 is beyond ODT\'s statutory authority to assess.

issue(1, "SUT-1 Cuyahoga County surtax base overstated by $35,600",
 "Notice §III.B and Schedule C-1 apply the 2.25% Cuyahoga rate to $623,000. Schedule C-2, ODT’s own invoice-level support, lists three Cuyahoga invoices totaling $587,400 ($214,800 + $198,600 + $174,000), and its county subtotal table also shows $587,400. The $35,600 difference equals invoice GS-21-0634 (Northfield Protective Products, Summit County). The same $623,000 figure appears in the Preliminary Findings, so the error was not corrected despite the intervening review.",
 "The Department’s narrative figure is contradicted by its own schedule. A Summit County sale cannot bear the Cuyahoga surtax. Note that ODT assessed no county tax on non-Cuyahoga sales; we do not recommend volunteering that point, but the Petition should be drafted so as not to invite a re-computation of county taxes in other counties (ODT’s ability to increase an assessment on petition should be confirmed).",
 "$801.00 tax + $80.10 penalty + $137.37 interest = $1,018.47 (subsumed if SUT-1 is withdrawn in full).",
 "Strong — documentary; ODT should concede.",
 "Plead as an alternative, computational ground in the Petition.")

issue(2, "SUT-1 rests on a self-defeating theory and inconsistent facts (four customers vs. ten)",
 "ODT’s finding is that the customers are \"retail resellers\" who \"purchase Greystone Shield Pro for resale to end users.\" Both the Preliminary Findings and Notice say four customers, but Schedule C-2 identifies ten different customers (one invoice each) across seven counties. The stated factual basis also changed between the Preliminary Findings (customers’ CAT filings and third-party verification) and the Notice (Secretary of State filings, public descriptions, A/R patterns). Greystone held exemption certificates for the customers; the Protest did not address SUT-1.",
 "(a) Sales to a purchaser who resells the product are sales for resale and are excluded from \"retail sale\" (R.C. 5739.01(E)(1) — confirm). ODT’s factual finding therefore supports exemption rather than tax; at most the certificates stated the wrong exemption reason. (b) A vendor that accepts a fully completed exemption certificate in good faith is relieved of liability, and Ohio provides a period after an auditor’s request in which the vendor may obtain a corrected certificate or other proof of exempt status (R.C. 5739.03(B) — confirm current subsection and the cure period). (c) The four-vs-ten customer conflict means the $1,847,500 base may include customers ODT never reclassified. (d) If any tax is ultimately due, the proper course is to collect from the purchasers who consumed the product, not to deem a reseller sale taxable.",
 "$120,248.75 tax + $12,024.88 penalty + $20,622.66 interest = $152,896.29.",
 "Moderate to Strong; depends on the certificates (form, completeness, exemption reason claimed) and customer resale evidence.",
 "Obtain all exemption/resale certificates and customer resale documentation now; consider obtaining corrected resale certificates from the customers; demand that ODT identify the \"four\" customers and reconcile to C-2; raise the issue in the Petition even though it was not protested (Greystone reserved new arguments).")

issue(3, "WHT-1 Schedule B-3 does not support the narrative (12 vs. 14 employees; different badge numbers)",
 "Narrative (§IV.B): 14 employees, wages $762,400 (2021) + $485,200 (2022) = $1,247,600; deficiency $37,428.00. Schedule B-3: 12 employees, wages $735,500 + $469,100 = $1,204,600; deficiency $36,138.00. Unsupported: $26,900 (2021) + $16,100 (2022) = $43,000 of wages and $1,290.00 of deficiency. The Preliminary Findings badge list (14 numbers) shares only Badge 2104 with Schedule B-3; the other 11 B-3 badges (2287, 2419, 2563, 2681, 2745, 2898, 3012, 3156, 3244, 3478, 3592) do not appear in the Preliminary Findings list, and 13 of the 14 Preliminary Findings badges do not appear in B-3. The client tracker notes only that Badges 3387 and 3401 are missing, which understates the discrepancy.",
 "The Department cannot sustain wages it has not identified by employee, and the employee population itself is unreliable. This goes beyond the $43,000 gap: it calls into question whether the wages assessed relate to employees actually assigned to the AllBright project and to work days actually performed in Columbus.",
 "Minimum $1,290.00 tax + $322.50 penalty + $174.15 interest = $1,786.65; potentially the entire WHT-1 amount if ODT cannot reconcile the employee population.",
 "Strong as to the $43,000; supports a broader evidentiary challenge.",
 "Reconcile Greystone payroll (Exhibit D and IDR 3 response) to both badge lists; require ODT to produce employee-level support for all 14; compute actual Columbus work days per employee (including any days not worked on site).")

issue(4, "SUT-3: statute of limitations on Q1 2020 service revenue",
 "The Preliminary Findings disclosed quarterly 2020 service revenue (Q1 $31,400, return due April 23, 2020; Q2 $29,700, due July 23, 2020; Q3 $34,200, due Oct. 23, 2020; Q4 $36,800, due Jan. 23, 2021) and expressly noted that the return due dates \"determine the applicable assessment periods.\" The Notice states that \"no quarterly breakdown of the 2020 service revenue is provided\" and assesses 2020 as an annual lump sum. The Notice issued June 14, 2024.",
 "Ohio generally bars a sales tax assessment issued more than four years after the later of the return due date or filing date (R.C. 5739.16 — confirm). Q1 2020 (due April 23, 2020) fell outside four years on April 23, 2024; Q2 2020 (due July 23, 2020) was still open on June 14, 2024. Two qualifications must be resolved before relying on this: (i) 2020 Am. Sub. H.B. 197 tolled various Revised Code limitation periods from March 9 to July 30, 2020, which, if applicable to R.C. 5739.16, would push the Q1 2020 deadline to approximately July 30, 2024; and (ii) whether Greystone executed a limitations waiver/extension during the audit. The Notice’s suppression of the quarterly data ODT itself relied on in February 2024 is an independent ground to demand recomputation. The same analysis should be run for (a) CAT, if Greystone was a quarterly CAT filer (a taxpayer with taxable gross receipts above $1 million is ordinarily a quarterly filer — confirm against returns; the Notice treats Greystone as an annual filer with a May 10 due date), where the Q1 2020 return would have been due May 10, 2020; and (b) any SUT item for early-2020 periods.",
 "Q1 2020: $1,805.50 tax + $180.55 penalty + $372.84 interest = $2,358.89 (based on the Preliminary Findings quarterly figure).",
 "Moderate — strong on the face of the dates, subject to H.B. 197 tolling and any waiver.",
 "Confirm H.B. 197 applicability and waiver history; plead limitations in the Petition; request ODT’s quarterly workpapers for the $127,300 figure.")

The $4,800 reduction ($276.00 tax) does not correspond to any of the four quarters.",

The source of the Protest’s $127,300 figure should be confirmed internally before the Petition, since the client may have used a different revenue measure.",

issue(6, "SUT-2: Hartmann machine — inconsistent theories; no authority for pro-rata taxation; R&D use",
 "Preliminary Findings: equipment fails the \"primarily used\" test because use is 50/50, so 50% is taxed. Notice: R&D is \"separate from\" manufacturing and the exemption is applied \"on a pro-rata basis.\" The Notice also records that Greystone produced only \"partial usage logs\" in response to IDR 2 (§VI ¶4), yet the 50/50 split is presented as a finding.",
 "(a) A \"primarily used\" test is all-or-nothing; if the machine is not primarily used in manufacturing the result would be full taxation, and if it is (or if R&D is part of manufacturing) the result is full exemption — the statute does not provide for apportionment (R.C. 5739.011 — confirm). (b) Under ODT’s own 50/50 finding, a tie is not resolved in ODT’s favor without authority. (c) Independent of § 5739.011, Ohio separately exempts tangible personal property used primarily in research and development (R.C. 5739.02(B)(42) — confirm subsection); if both the production and R&D uses are exempt, the machine is 100% exempt regardless of the split. (d) The Protest’s reliance on Ohio Adm.Code 5703-9-21 (quality control/testing as part of manufacturing) was not answered. (e) The 50% split derives from partial logs; the full-period usage data should be developed. (f) Interest runs from the purchase/installation date (Nov. 30, 2021) rather than the due date of the return on which use tax would have been reported. (g) The 10% penalty is cited under R.C. 5739.13, the vendor statute; consumer use tax is assessed under R.C. Chapter 5741 (§ 5741.13 — confirm).",
 "$78,975.00 tax + $7,897.50 penalty + $14,041.76 interest = $100,914.26.",
 "Moderate to Strong (particularly the R&D exemption and the absence of pro-rata authority).",
 "Engage Pinnacle to complete a usage study from complete logs; add the R&D exemption ground (not raised in the Protest); maintain the full-exemption position; alternatively challenge the 50% allocation and the interest start date.")

issue(7, "SUT-3: characterization of field-service activities",
 "ODT describes on-site installation of coating systems, calibration of application equipment and repair of installed coatings. Greystone’s Protest describes technicians who supervise and advise customers on surface preparation and application, billed as technician time and travel — i.e., non-enumerated consulting services. ODT’s §VII.C states that the Code has no exception for services incidental to a sale.",
 "This is a fact dispute that the Petition must resolve with evidence (Exhibit C work orders, contracts, invoices). Additional grounds to develop: (a) coatings applied to customers’ real property may constitute construction-contract activity or services to realty rather than installation/repair of tangible personal property (R.C. 5739.01(B)(3) and (Y) — confirm); (b) consulting/supervisory time is not an enumerated taxable service; (c) to the extent installation charges were part of a taxable sale of tangible personal property, tax may already have been addressed on the product price (confirm treatment). If any portion is sustained, the 2020 limitations point (Issue 4) and base reconciliation (Issue 5) still apply.",
 "$23,736.00 tax + $2,373.60 penalty + $4,901.58 interest = $31,011.18.",
 "Moderate — evidence-dependent.",
 "Collect representative work orders by activity type and segregate revenue among (i) consulting/supervision, (ii) realty-related application, and (iii) equipment calibration/repair; challenge at least categories (i) and (ii).")

issue(8, "SUT-4: 50% \"enhanced\" penalty unsupported by findings",
 "The Preliminary Findings deferred the \"appropriate penalty classification.\" The Notice imposes 50% \"due to the discrepancy between collected and remitted amounts,\" citing \"O.R.C. § 5739.13 et seq.,\" without any finding of intent, fraud or wilful conduct, and without identifying the subsection. The client tracker records the rate as an \"enhanced ‘fraud’ rate.\"",
 "The penalty schedule for vendors appears in R.C. 5739.133 (confirm the tiers and whether a higher tier is discretionary or requires specific findings). A bare arithmetic difference is not a finding of culpable conduct, and the Notice does not consider explanations such as timing (amounts remitted in a later period), refunds/credit memos to customers, bad debts, or overpayments in other quarters that should be netted. The tax itself (collected funds) is harder to contest, and Ohio may require payment of collected-but-unremitted tax as a condition of the petition (R.C. 5739.13(B) — confirm).",
 "Penalty $10,747.50; excess over the 10% rate applied to other items = $8,598.00. Tax $21,495.00 and interest $2,437.53 likely payable.",
 "Moderate to Strong on penalty; Weak on tax unless reconciliation shows remittance in another period.",
 "Reconcile Q3 2022 GL, sales journal, return and bank deposits; consider paying the SUT-4 tax with the petition to stop interest and satisfy any prepayment condition; seek penalty reduction/abatement.")

issue(9, "Procedural defect: no response to Protest Argument 1 (CAT intercompany management fees)",
 "§VII.A lists four arguments; §§VII.B–D address only Arguments 2, 3 and 4. Argument 1 — the related-member exclusion for $12,075,000 of management fees — receives no response, although the cover letter recites that the Department \"considered all ... protests.\" The Notice also (i) states the protest was prepared by Ms. Navarro, when it was signed by Ms. Chen, and (ii) does not reflect the conference Greystone requested.",
 "Failure to address a timely protest argument undermines the reasoned-determination presumption and should be emphasized in the Petition; it may also support a request that the Tax Commissioner hold the requested hearing (R.C. 5703.60 / petition hearing rights — confirm). Substantively: (a) the out-of-state organization of the subsidiaries is not itself the statutory test — exclusions for intra-group receipts depend on ownership and group composition (consolidated elected / combined taxpayer group, R.C. 5751.01(F)(2)(c), 5751.011, 5751.012 — confirm; the Protest’s citation to 5751.01(F)(2)(ll) should be re-verified before re-use); (b) even if not excluded, receipts from services are sitused where the purchaser receives the benefit (R.C. 5751.033(I) — confirm); management services consumed by Georgia and Nevada distribution subsidiaries are received outside Ohio, and the Preliminary Findings’ \"services performed in Ohio\" test is the wrong test. The Notice does not analyze situs at all.",
 "Management-fee share of CAT: 2020 $14,397.94; 2021 $12,218.21; 2022 $12,911.17 = $39,527.32 (tax $31,395.00; penalty $4,709.25; interest $3,423.07). Note: the Protest overstated this point as $53,531.50, which includes the Canadian licensing receipts.",
 "Moderate (exclusion) and Moderate to Strong (situs); procedural point Strong.",
 "Re-plead both exclusion and situs; obtain intercompany agreements and transfer-pricing support showing where the benefit of services is received; correct the amount claimed.")

issue(10, "WHT-1: ODT lacks authority over the Columbus municipal component; school district component misdirected",
 "The Notice assesses $31,190.00 of Columbus municipal income tax and $6,238.00 of Columbus City School District income tax. §VII.D responds to the jurisdiction argument only by describing a \"coordinated audit\" and inviting the taxpayer to pursue \"appropriate administrative channels\"; it cites no authority. The Notice’s cover letter cites Chapters 5733, 5739, 5741, 5747 and 5751 but not Chapter 718.",
 "(a) Municipal: Columbus administers its own income tax (Columbus Income Tax Division) under R.C. Chapter 718; ODT’s role in municipal taxes is limited to the centralized net-profit filing regime for electing businesses (R.C. 718.80 et seq. — confirm), which does not extend to employer withholding. The municipal component, with its penalty and interest, should be withdrawn in full. Separately, Greystone should evaluate exposure directly to Columbus (20-day occasional-entrant rule, R.C. 718.011 — confirm) and the corresponding refund/credit of Richfield tax over-withheld on the same wages. (b) School district: Ohio school district income tax is imposed on residents of the district and employer withholding is based on the employee’s residence, not work location (R.C. Chapter 5748; 5747.06 — confirm). The Notice assumes withholding is owed because the employees worked in Columbus; it does not find that any employee resided in the Columbus City School District. We also understand that Columbus City School District may not levy a school district income tax at all (confirm against ODT’s SDIT rate tables). The Protest’s concession of ODT jurisdiction over the SD component does not concede liability and the point should be raised. (c) The midpoint used for interest (Oct. 1, 2021) is about one month before the actual midpoint of a March 2021–June 2022 assignment (≈ Nov. 1, 2021; overstatement ≈ $149.71), and interest should run from the withholding-return due dates. (d) The 5% WHT interest rate differs from the 7% SUT rate for overlapping periods (Issue 13).",
 "Municipal: $31,190.00 + $7,797.50 + $4,210.65 = $43,198.15. School district: $6,238.00 + $1,559.50 + $842.13 = $8,639.63. Total WHT-1: $51,837.78.",
 "Strong (municipal); Moderate to Strong (school district).",
 "Plead lack of authority for the municipal component; obtain employee residence addresses for all assigned employees; confirm whether Columbus City SD levies an income tax.")

issue(11, "CAT Canadian licensing receipts: situs not analyzed; never protested; orphan footnote",
 "The Preliminary Findings sitused the licensing receipts to Ohio under R.C. 5751.033 because the IP was \"developed and managed\" in Ohio. The Notice drops the situs analysis and simply concludes the receipts are \"sitused to Ohio.\" Greystone’s Protest did not contest these receipts. Schedule C-1 footnote 1 states that only $418,000 of 2022 \"foreign licensing revenue\" is a \"taxable portion ... attributable to tangible personal property transferred,\" citing IDR 3 materials; no SUT item uses this figure and Schedule A-1 taxes the full $2,290,000.",
 "Receipts from the use of intangible property are sitused to Ohio to the extent the receipts are based on the right to use the property in Ohio (R.C. 5751.033(F) — confirm). A Canadian distributor’s use of formulas in Canada is not Ohio use; the place of development is irrelevant under that rule. The footnote suggests ODT itself distinguished between intangible and tangible elements of the arrangement and may evidence that the bulk of the receipts are intangible licence fees with no Ohio use. The footnote must be explained by ODT. Greystone reserved the right to raise new arguments, so failure to protest should not bar this ground in the Petition (confirm).",
 "2021 $6,827.82 + 2022 $7,176.36 = $14,004.18 (tax $11,388.00; penalty $1,708.20; interest $907.98).",
 "Moderate to Strong, subject to the terms of the licensing agreement (territory of use).",
 "Obtain the licensing agreement and royalty reports; add as a new ground; demand explanation of the C-1 footnote and the IDR 3 reference.")

issue(12, "Penalties: generic citations; abatement grounds",
 "CAT 15% penalty is cited only to \"applicable provisions of Ohio law\"; the WHT 25% penalty to \"applicable withholding penalty provisions\"; the SUT 10% penalty to R.C. 5739.13 for all three items (including the use-tax item SUT-2). No statute, rate tier or discretionary findings are identified.",
 "The Notice must identify the authority for each penalty so it can be contested; the Tax Commissioner has discretion to abate penalties (confirm under R.C. 5751.06, 5739.133, 5747.15 and related provisions). Grounds: good-faith, consistently applied reporting positions supported by reasonable legal interpretation (CAT, SUT-2, SUT-3); reliance on exemption certificates (SUT-1); full cooperation with the audit, which the Preliminary Findings expressly acknowledged.",
 "Total penalties $48,817.93.",
 "Moderate.",

issue(1, "SUT-1 Cuyahoga County surtax base overstated by $35,600",
 "Notice §III.B and Schedule C-1 apply the 2.25% Cuyahoga rate to $623,000. Schedule C-2, ODT\u2019s own invoice-level support, lists three Cuyahoga invoices totaling $587,400 ($214,800 + $198,600 + $174,000), and its county subtotal table also shows $587,400. The $35,600 difference equals invoice GS-21-0634 (Northfield Protective Products, Summit County). The same $623,000 figure appears in the Preliminary Findings, so the error was not corrected despite the intervening review.",
 "The Department\u2019s narrative figure is contradicted by its own schedule. A Summit County sale cannot bear the Cuyahoga surtax. Note that ODT assessed no county tax on non-Cuyahoga sales; we do not recommend volunteering that point, but the Petition should be drafted so as not to invite a re-computation of county taxes in other counties (ODT\u2019s ability to increase an assessment on petition should be confirmed).",
 "$801.00 tax + $80.10 penalty + $137.37 interest = $1,018.47 (subsumed if SUT-1 is withdrawn in full).",
 "Strong — documentary; ODT should concede.",
 "Plead as an alternative, computational ground in the Petition.")

issue(2, "SUT-1 rests on a self-defeating theory and inconsistent facts (four customers vs. ten)",
 "ODT\u2019s finding is that the customers are \"retail resellers\" who \"purchase Greystone Shield Pro for resale to end users.\" Both the Preliminary Findings and Notice say four customers, but Schedule C-2 identifies ten different customers (one invoice each) across seven counties. The stated factual basis also changed between the Preliminary Findings (customers\u2019 CAT filings and third-party verification) and the Notice (Secretary of State filings, public descriptions, A/R patterns). Greystone held exemption certificates for the customers; the Protest did not address SUT-1.",
 "(a) Sales to a purchaser who resells the product are sales for resale and are excluded from \"retail sale\" (R.C. 5739.01(E)(1) — confirm). ODT\u2019s factual finding therefore supports exemption rather than tax; at most the certificates stated the wrong exemption reason. (b) A vendor that accepts a fully completed exemption certificate in good faith is relieved of liability, and Ohio provides a period after an auditor\u2019s request in which the vendor may obtain a corrected certificate or other proof of exempt status (R.C. 5739.03(B) — confirm current subsection and the cure period). (c) The four-vs-ten customer conflict means the $1,847,500 base may include customers ODT never reclassified. (d) If any tax is ultimately due, the proper course is to collect from the purchasers who consumed the product, not to deem a reseller sale taxable.",
 "$120,248.75 tax + $12,024.88 penalty + $20,622.66 interest = $152,896.29.",
 "Moderate to Strong; depends on the certificates (form, completeness, exemption reason claimed) and customer resale evidence.",
 "Obtain all exemption/resale certificates and customer resale documentation now; consider obtaining corrected resale certificates from the customers; demand that ODT identify the \"four\" customers and reconcile to C-2; raise the issue in the Petition even though it was not protested (Greystone reserved new arguments).")

Schedule B-3: 12 employees, wages $735,500 + $469,100 = $1,204,600; deficiency $36,138.00. Unsupported: $26,900 (2021) + $16,100 (2022) = $43,000 of wages and $1,290.00 of deficiency. The Preliminary Findings badge list (14 numbers) shares only Badge 2104 with Schedule B-3; the other 11 B-3 badges (2287, 2419, 2563, 2681, 2745, 2898, 3012, 3156, 3244, 3478, 3592) do not appear in the Preliminary Findings list, and 13 of the 14 Preliminary Findings badges do not appear in B-3. The client tracker notes only that Badges 3387 and 3401 are missing, which understates the discrepancy.",

This goes beyond the $43,000 gap: it calls into question whether the wages assessed relate to employees actually assigned to the AllBright project and to work days actually performed in Columbus.",

issue(4, "SUT-3: statute of limitations on Q1 2020 service revenue",
 "The Preliminary Findings disclosed quarterly 2020 service revenue (Q1 $31,400, return due April 23, 2020; Q2 $29,700, due July 23, 2020; Q3 $34,200, due Oct. 23, 2020; Q4 $36,800, due Jan. 23, 2021) and expressly noted that the return due dates \"determine the applicable assessment periods.\" The Notice states that \"no quarterly breakdown of the 2020 service revenue is provided\" and assesses 2020 as an annual lump sum. The Notice issued June 14, 2024.",
 "Ohio generally bars a sales tax assessment issued more than four years after the later of the return due date or filing date (R.C. 5739.16 — confirm). Q1 2020 (due April 23, 2020) fell outside four years on April 23, 2024; Q2 2020 (due July 23, 2020) was still open on June 14, 2024. Two qualifications must be resolved before relying on this: (i) 2020 Am. Sub. H.B. 197 tolled various Revised Code limitation periods from March 9 to July 30, 2020, which, if applicable to R.C. 5739.16, would push the Q1 2020 deadline to approximately July 30, 2024; and (ii) whether Greystone executed a limitations waiver/extension during the audit. The Notice\u2019s suppression of the quarterly data ODT itself relied on in February 2024 is an independent ground to demand recomputation. The same analysis should be run for (a) CAT, if Greystone was a quarterly CAT filer (a taxpayer with taxable gross receipts above $1 million is ordinarily a quarterly filer — confirm against returns; the Notice treats Greystone as an annual filer with a May 10 due date), where the Q1 2020 return would have been due May 10, 2020; and (b) any SUT item for early-2020 periods.",
 "Q1 2020: $1,805.50 tax + $180.55 penalty + $372.84 interest = $2,358.89 (based on the Preliminary Findings quarterly figure).",
 "Moderate — strong on the face of the dates, subject to H.B. 197 tolling and any waiver.",
 "Confirm H.B. 197 applicability and waiver history; plead limitations in the Petition; request ODT\u2019s quarterly workpapers for the $127,300 figure.")

issue(6, "SUT-2: Hartmann machine — inconsistent theories; no authority for pro-rata taxation; R&D use",
 "Preliminary Findings: equipment fails the \"primarily used\" test because use is 50/50, so 50% is taxed. Notice: R&D is \"separate from\" manufacturing and the exemption is applied \"on a pro-rata basis.\" The Notice also records that Greystone produced only \"partial usage logs\" in response to IDR 2 (§VI ¶4), yet the 50/50 split is presented as a finding.",
 "(a) A \"primarily used\" test is all-or-nothing; if the machine is not primarily used in manufacturing the result would be full taxation, and if it is (or if R&D is part of manufacturing) the result is full exemption — the statute does not provide for apportionment (R.C. 5739.011 — confirm). (b) Under ODT\u2019s own 50/50 finding, a tie is not resolved in ODT\u2019s favor without authority. (c) Independent of § 5739.011, Ohio separately exempts tangible personal property used primarily in research and development (R.C. 5739.02(B)(42) — confirm subsection); if both the production and R&D uses are exempt, the machine is 100% exempt regardless of the split. (d) The Protest\u2019s reliance on Ohio Adm.Code 5703-9-21 (quality control/testing as part of manufacturing) was not answered. (e) The 50% split derives from partial logs; the full-period usage data should be developed. (f) Interest runs from the purchase/installation date (Nov. 30, 2021) rather than the due date of the return on which use tax would have been reported. (g) The 10% penalty is cited under R.C. 5739.13, the vendor statute; consumer use tax is assessed under R.C. Chapter 5741 (§ 5741.13 — confirm).",
 "$78,975.00 tax + $7,897.50 penalty + $14,041.76 interest = $100,914.26.",
 "Moderate to Strong (particularly the R&D exemption and the absence of pro-rata authority).",
 "Engage Pinnacle to complete a usage study from complete logs; add the R&D exemption ground (not raised in the Protest); maintain the full-exemption position; alternatively challenge the 50% allocation and the interest start date.")

issue(9, "Procedural defect: no response to Protest Argument 1 (CAT intercompany management fees)",
 "§VII.A lists four arguments; §§VII.B–D address only Arguments 2, 3 and 4. Argument 1 — the related-member exclusion for $12,075,000 of management fees — receives no response, although the cover letter recites that the Department \"considered all ... protests.\" The Notice also (i) states the protest was prepared by Ms. Navarro, when it was signed by Ms. Chen, and (ii) does not reflect the conference Greystone requested.",
 "Failure to address a timely protest argument undermines the reasoned-determination presumption and should be emphasized in the Petition; it may also support a request that the Tax Commissioner hold the requested hearing (R.C. 5703.60 / petition hearing rights — confirm). Substantively: (a) the out-of-state organization of the subsidiaries is not itself the statutory test — exclusions for intra-group receipts depend on ownership and group composition (consolidated elected / combined taxpayer group, R.C. 5751.01(F)(2)(c), 5751.011, 5751.012 — confirm; the Protest\u2019s citation to 5751.01(F)(2)(ll) should be re-verified before re-use); (b) even if not excluded, receipts from services are sitused where the purchaser receives the benefit (R.C. 5751.033(I) — confirm); management services consumed by Georgia and Nevada distribution subsidiaries are received outside Ohio, and the Preliminary Findings\u2019 \"services performed in Ohio\" test is the wrong test. The Notice does not analyze situs at all.",

*Prepared at the direction of counsel; Pinnacle Tax Advisors LLC participation under Kovel arrangement*

Tax Assessment Extraction and Verification Report

**Greystone Industrial Holdings, Inc. --- Ohio Department of Taxation Final Assessment Notice dated June 14, 2024**

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Field**                           **Detail**
  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  To                                  Patricia Navarro, Partner, Braddock & Lyle LLP

  Client                              Greystone Industrial Holdings, Inc. (FEIN 34-1987652; Ohio Tax ID 00-874231), 4510 Brecksville Road, Suite 300, Richfield, Ohio 44286; client contact Victoria Chen, VP of Tax

  Matter                              Review of ODT Final Assessment Notice, Assessment Case No. ODT-AUD-2023-07814 (Engagement Scope Items 1--4, engagement email of June 20, 2024)

  Assessment total per notice         \$424,871.04 (deficiency \$324,665.75; penalties \$48,817.93; interest \$51,387.36)

  Critical deadline                   Petition for Reassessment and payment / bond / stay: on or before August 13, 2024 (60 days from June 14, 2024, as stated in the notice). Internal target for this report: July 19, 2024.

  Status                              Draft for partner review. Legal positions flagged \"confirm\" require statutory/authority verification (B&L research / Pinnacle) before use in the Petition.
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Executive Summary

We extracted every assessed item from the Final Assessment Notice (the \"Notice\") and its Schedules A-1, B-3, C-1, C-2 and C-4, independently recomputed every figure, and cross-referenced the Notice against the ODT Preliminary Findings letter (February 12, 2024), Greystone's Protest letter (March 28, 2024), the engagement email (June 20, 2024), and Greystone's internal tax-assessment tracker (prepared June 24, 2024). The headline totals in the Notice foot and cross-foot correctly, but the supporting schedules do not support several of the narrative figures, the interest computations use three different rates and two different methods for overlapping periods, and the Notice fails to respond at all to one of Greystone's four protest arguments. Key conclusions:

- **Overall:** Every item in the Notice (\$424,871.04) is contested or contestable to some degree. We recommend a timely Petition for Reassessment covering all items, with the strongest challenges directed at WHT-1 (municipal component), SUT-1, SUT-2, the CAT management-fee and Canadian licensing situsing, the SUT-4 50% penalty, and the interest methodology.

- **Computational and schedule errors confirmed:** (a) Schedule C-2 Cuyahoga County invoices total \$587,400, not the \$623,000 used to compute the county surtax (overstatement \$35,600 of base / \$801.00 tax, \$1,018.47 with penalty and interest); (b) Schedule B-3 lists only 12 employees and \$1,204,600 of wages versus 14 employees and \$1,247,600 in the narrative (unsupported wages \$43,000 / \$1,290.00 deficiency, \$1,786.65 with penalty and interest), and 11 of the 12 Schedule B-3 badge numbers do not match the 14 badge numbers listed in the Preliminary Findings; (c) Schedule A-1 compound-interest factors are misstated for all three CAT years; (d) SUT-3 interest is overstated by \$0.10 (arithmetic error); (e) Schedule C-2 identifies ten different customers, while the Notice and Preliminary Findings describe SUT-1 as sales to four customers.

- **Procedural defects:** The Notice's Section VII lists all four protest arguments but responds only to Arguments 2, 3 and 4; there is no response to Argument 1 (CAT related-member exclusion for \$12,075,000 of management fees). The Notice also misattributes the protest to Ms. Navarro (it was signed by Ms. Chen), and does not indicate that the conference Greystone requested was held.

- **Statute of limitations:** The Notice reduced SUT-3 2020 service revenue from \$132,100 (Preliminary Findings) to \$127,300 without explanation and dropped the quarterly breakdown that the Preliminary Findings provided. The Preliminary Findings show Q1 2020 service revenue of \$31,400 on a return due April 23, 2020 --- more than four years before the June 14, 2024 assessment. Subject to confirming the effect of the 2020 COVID-19 tolling legislation (H.B. 197) and whether Greystone signed any limitations waiver, this portion appears time-barred.

- **Substantive theory problems:** SUT-1 rests on an internally contradictory theory: if the four customers are \"retail resellers\" (ODT's finding), their purchases are sales for resale, which are not taxable retail sales to Greystone's customers. The WHT-1 school district component appears to rest on the wrong nexus (work location rather than employee residence), and the municipal component is outside ODT's administrative authority (City of Columbus administers its own tax under R.C. Chapter 718).

- **Petition mechanics:** The Notice, the engagement email and the tracker all cite R.C. 5717.02 as the basis of the Petition for Reassessment. R.C. 5717.02 governs appeals to the Board of Tax Appeals; the petition provisions are tax-specific (e.g., R.C. 5739.13 (sales/use), 5747.13 (withholding), 5751.09 (CAT)) (confirm). The petition should cite the correct provisions. The Notice is also internally inconsistent on whether payment is due if a petition is filed (cover letter vs. Section VIII); and for collected-but-unremitted tax (SUT-4) Ohio may require payment of that portion with the petition (confirm).

I finished the Greystone assessment report. It has every assessed item from ODT's June 14, 2024 final notice, my own recomputation of each figure, and a check against the preliminary findings, the protest letter, the engagement email and the client's tracker. The headline total of $424,871.04 adds up correctly. The problems are in the schedules and legal grounds behind it. The file passes validation and reads back correctly.

- **Calculation errors:**
  - Schedule C-2 supports only $587,400 of Cuyahoga County sales, not the $623,000 taxed (the gap is a Summit County invoice). That overstates the tax by $801.
  - Schedule B-3 lists 12 employees and $1,204,600 of wages, against 14 employees and $1,247,600 in the text. Only one badge number matches the preliminary findings' list.
  - All three CAT interest factors are wrong.
  - The SUT-3 interest is off by $0.10.
  - Correcting these alone takes $2,792.49 off the total.
- **Notice defects:**
  - ODT never answers protest argument 1 (CAT management fees).
  - It says Patricia Navarro wrote the protest; Victoria Chen signed it.
  - It cites R.C. 5717.02 for the Petition for Reassessment, which is the appeal statute (the tracker and engagement email repeat this).
  - It contradicts itself on whether payment is due if a petition is filed.
  - Schedule C-1 has a footnote ($418,000) that nothing in the notice refers to.
- **Grounds to challenge:**
  - **SUT-3:** the 2020 base was cut by $4,800 without explanation, and the quarterly breakdown was dropped. Q1 2020 may be past the four-year limit, unless the 2020 COVID tolling law or a signed waiver applies.
  - **SUT-1:** ODT's own finding that the customers are resellers undercuts the tax, and its schedule shows 10 customers, not 4.
  - **SUT-2:** there is no authority for taxing half the Hartmann machine, and a separate R&D exemption may apply.
  - **CAT:** situs rules may move the management fees and Canadian licensing income outside Ohio. The licensing income was never protested.
  - **WHT-1:** ODT has no authority over Columbus municipal tax. The school district part is based on work location, but that tax follows where employees live.
  - **Penalties and interest:** nothing supports the 50% SUT-4 penalty, and the interest uses different rates and methods for the same period.

I haven't checked the Ohio law points against current authority; they're marked "confirm" in the report. That includes the 2020 tolling question, the R&D exemption, the CAT situs rules and the interest rates, and they need checking before anything goes into the petition. The IDRs, the client's responses and the protest exhibits weren't in the file, so the report lists them as documents to request.
